blocks.text: And Apuleius, in book 3 of the Metamorphoses, says of eagle owls: “What of the fact that we see these night birds, when they have entered some house, carefully caught and nailed to the doors, so that by their own torments they may atone for the ruin which they threaten the family with their ill-omened flights?” Now, if you consult the historians: in Dio, at the death of Augustus, when the Senate had decreed that public supplications be made on account of his health, τότε συνέδριον κεκλεισμένον εὑρέθη, καὶ βύας, ὑπερ αὐτου καθήμενος, ἔβυξε [tote synedrion kekleismenon heurethē, kai byas, hyper autou kathēmenos, ebyxe], “the senate house was found shut, and an eagle owl, which had settled upon it, hooted.” And at the death of Commodus, Βύας ἀπ' αὐτου (Καπιτωλίου) ἔβυξε [Byas ap' autou (Kapitōliou) ebyxe], “An eagle owl hooted from the Capitol.” So too that very Herod Agrippa who at Caesarea was hailed as a god by the frenzied populace, Act. XII, 22: ἀνακύψας μετ' ὀλίγον, τὸν βουβῶνα τῆς ἑαυτου κεφαλῆς ὑπερκαθεζόμενον εἶδεν ἐπὶ σχοινίου τινὸς, ἄγγελον τοῦτον εὐθὺς ἐνόησεν κακῶν εἶναι, τὸν καὶ πότε τῶν ἀγαθῶν γενόμενον [anakypsas met' oligon, ton boubōna tēs heautou kephalēs hyperkathezomenon eiden epi schoiniou tinos, angelon touton euthys enoēsen kakōn einai, ton kai pote tōn agathōn genomenon], “looking up a little later, he saw an eagle owl above his head, sitting on a rope, and he perceived that it was a messenger of evil, as it had once been of good.” For formerly, when by order of Gaius Caligula he had been bound and was leaning against a tree on which an eagle owl had settled, a certain German had foretold that shortly, with a change of fortune, he would be raised to the highest dignity. “But remember,” he said, ὁπότε εἰς αὖθις τὸν ὄρνιν θεάσαιο τοῦτον, πέντε ἡμέραις σοι τὴν τελευτὴν ἐσομένην [hopote eis authis ton ornin theasaio touton, pente hēmerais soi tēn teleutēn esomenēn], “whenever you see this bird again, you will die within five days.” Both accounts are read in Josephus, book 18, chapter 8, and book 19, chapter 7. Hence it is clear why Agrippa, when about to die, said that the same eagle owl was an ἄγγελον [angelon], or messenger, of evil which had once been one of good. Yet Eusebius transcribed this passage of Josephus thus: Ἀνακύψας δὲ μετ' ὀλίγον τῆς ἑαυτου κεφαλῆς ὑπερκαθεζόμενον εἶδεν ἄγγελον [Anakypsas de met' oligon tēs heautou kephalēs hyperkathezomenon eiden angelon], omitting the mention of the eagle owl, as if that angel were meant by whom the king is read to have been struck, Actor. XII, 23, which is no slight παρόραμα [parorama].
